title: Superconductivity and local stacking polymorphism in LaNiGa2 thin films
authors: Pengcheng Wang, Qingxiao Wang, Yameng Wu, Zixuan Huang, C. T. Lam, Zheyu Wang, Swee K. Goh, Xiaoying Xu, Yufan Li
abstract: LaNiGa2 has attracted considerable interest as a candidate unconventional superconductor, particularly due to its reported time-reversal symmetry breaking and nonsymmorphic crystal structure hosting symmetry-protected electronic band degeneracies. Here, we report the growth and characterization of superconducting LaNiGa2 thin films on MgO substrates by magnetron sputtering. X-ray diffraction reveals highly crystalline, (010)-oriented films with well-defined in-plane alignment and rotational twinning. Electrical transport measurements establish superconductivity with a transition temperature of approximately 1 K. Atomic-resolution transmission electron microscopy reveals local variations in crystallographic orientation and interlayer stacking, with a predominantly Cmcm structure containing minority Cmmm regions. The coexistence of these closely related structures reveals local stacking polymorphism that is difficult to distinguish using conventional X-ray diffraction. These findings establish a superconducting LaNiGa2 thin-film platform and provide new insight into the local crystal structure of a material whose electronic properties and superconducting pairing remain under active investigation.
summary: This work reports on the growth and characterization of superconducting LaNiGa2 thin films, confirming superconductivity at $\sim 1 	ext{ K}$. Crucially, atomic-resolution TEM reveals that the film exhibits local stacking polymorphism, coexisting between $	ext{Cmcm}$ and $	ext{Cmmm}$ crystal structures. This finding suggests that local structural details, rather than just the average crystal structure, govern the material's electronic and superconducting behavior.
main_problem: The study investigates the interplay between superconductivity and local stacking polymorphism in LaNiGa2 thin films.
main_result: The films exhibit superconductivity ($T_c \approx 1 	ext{ K}$) and show local structural variations, coexisting between the $	ext{Cmcm}$ and $	ext{Cmmm}$ crystal structures, which is difficult to detect with conventional XRD.
method: The research combines magnetron sputtering for film growth, electrical transport measurements, and atomic-resolution transmission electron microscopy (STEM) to characterize the structure.
model_or_system: The physical system is superconducting LaNiGa2 thin films grown epitaxially on MgO substrates. The analysis compares the structural motifs of two closely related space groups, $	ext{Cmcm}$ and $	ext{Cmmm}$, which govern the local stacking arrangement.
key_observables: Superconducting transition temperature ($T_c \approx 0.96 	ext{ K}$), crystallographic orientation ($	ext{(010)}$), and the coexistence of $	ext{Cmcm}$ and $	ext{Cmmm}$ local stacking domains.
important_parameters: Superconducting transition temperature ($\approx 1 	ext{ K}$); energy difference between structural variants ($	ext{Cmmm}$ calculated to be $12.7 	ext{ meV/atom}$ lower than $	ext{Cmcm}$).
main_assumptions: The local structural variations observed via TEM are representative of the electronic structure influencing superconductivity, despite the near-identical lattice parameters of the two phases.
figures_summary: Figures show XRD scans confirming $	ext{(010)}$ orientation and $\phi$ scans detailing rotational twinning. STEM images illustrate the coexistence of $	ext{Cmcm}$ and $	ext{Cmmm}$ stacking motifs, while resistivity curves confirm the superconducting transition.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the superconducting nature and crystalline growth of the films using XRD and transport measurements. It then employs atomic-resolution TEM to reveal the subtle, local structural variations (stacking polymorphism) between the $	ext{Cmcm}$ and $	ext{Cmmm}$ phases, linking this structural heterogeneity to the material's electronic properties.
why_interesting: The investigation into how subtle, local structural variations (polymorphism) dictate the electronic and superconducting properties of a material is highly relevant to understanding emergent quantum phenomena in strongly correlated systems.
